openQuestions.text: What is git 2.50.1's documented daemon lifecycle on macOS? Does a daemon ever exit on its own, and how do fsmonitor.socketDir, idle shutdown and git fsmonitor--daemon stop behave when the daemon is wedged?
Is event overload the real cause of the hang, or is there a known daemon deadlock in this git version, for example around --ipc-threads or the cookie-file handshake?
What is the safest default: fsmonitor on with worktrees outside the checkout, or fsmonitor off for the main checkout and on per worktree?

The 2.50.1 manual documents exactly four subcommands (`start`, `run`, `stop`, `status`) and describes the daemon as "a long running process used to watch a single working directory". It documents no idle timeout, no lifetime bound, no self-exit and no TTL. [SOURCE: man git-fsmonitor--daemon, Git 2.50.1.428.g0e8243]

The manual documents the daemon only as "a long running process used to watch a single working directory", with `start`, `run`, `stop`, `status` — no idle timeout, no lifetime bound, no self-exit condition. [SOURCE: man git-fsmonitor--daemon (Git 2.50.1)]

The trigger is a lost cookie event, and the source names the mechanism: the cookie's open()/unlink() "will cause at least two FS events on that path, so the odds of getting stuck are pretty slim" — but a daemon watching roughly 2.5M files (including 93 `node_modules` trees under `.worktrees/`) can drop one under load, and one undelivered event parks one worker forever; eight parked clients saturate the pool so `status` and `stop` stop answering too. [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:206-212] [SOURCE: specs/sk-git/035-fsmonitor-daemon-and-worktree-relocation-regression/scratch/findings.md]

Upgrading is not the fix path: the 2.51.0, 2.52.0 and 2.53.0 release notes contain zero fsmonitor entries, so no announced change addresses the unbounded cookie wait or the client's unbounded read. [SOURCE: Documentation/RelNotes/2.51.0.adoc] [SOURCE: Documentation/RelNotes/2.52.0.adoc] [SOURCE: Documentation/RelNotes/2.53.0.adoc]

Because the Darwin health thread is a no-op and no idle exit exists, a daemon cannot retire itself. The 08:51:33 daemon (PID 17228) vanishing at 09:17:59 and being replaced by PID 18482 within a second therefore points at a signal or a crash, not at a timeout — the replacement is exactly what a client-start after a dead socket looks like. [INFERENCE: from findings 4-5] [SOURCE: specs/sk-git/035-fsmonitor-daemon-and-worktree-relocation-regression/scratch/findings.md]

Each blocked client holds one of the 8 IPC workers. Once the pool is saturated the daemon also stops answering `status` and `stop`, which is why the whole checkout looks frozen instead of one command looking slow, and why killing the daemon was the only thing that released the hook. [INFERENCE: from findings 2 and 6-7]

`fsmonitor.socketDir` only relocates the Unix socket when `.git` (or `$HOME`) is on a network-mounted filesystem; it has no bearing on lifecycle or on a native-filesystem checkout like this one. [SOURCE: man git-fsmonitor--daemon (Git 2.50.1)]

`--ipc-threads=8` in every live process is git's own compiled default, not this repo's configuration: `static int fsmonitor__ipc_threads = 8;` is the default for `fsmonitor.ipcthreads`, and this checkout sets no `fsmonitor.*` key at all. The argument is how the daemon re-execs itself into `run`, so it carries no signal about repo config. [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:35-52] [SOURCE: git config --show-origin --get-regexp, iteration 1]

On macOS the health thread is an empty stub: `fsm_health__ctor`, `fsm_health__loop` and `fsm_health__stop_async` all return immediately, while the header contract says the health thread "should call `ipc_server_stop_async()` if it needs to cause a shutdown". The daemon therefore never monitors its own liveness and never exits on health grounds on this platform. [SOURCE: compat/fsmonitor/fsm-health-darwin.c:8-27] [SOURCE: compat/fsmonitor/fsm-health.h:31-45]

The only timeout anywhere in the daemon's lifecycle is `fsmonitor.starttimeout` (default 60 s), and it bounds startup only — how long `start` waits for the background daemon to reach `IPC_STATE__LISTENING`. Nothing bounds a request. [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:38-61,1510]

`git fsmonitor--daemon stop` sends `quit` and then polls `fsmonitor_ipc__get_state() == IPC_STATE__LISTENING` every 50 ms with no deadline (`do_as_client__send_stop`), so on a daemon that cannot answer the stop command hangs — matching the packet's observed 15-second kill. [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:84-101]

On macOS the health thread is a complete no-op: `fsm_health__ctor()`, `fsm_health__loop()` and `fsm_health__stop_async()` all return immediately, so the daemon does not monitor its own listener, does not detect a stalled FSEvents stream, and never shuts itself down on health grounds. [SOURCE: compat/fsmonitor/fsm-health-darwin.c:1-28] [SOURCE: compat/fsmonitor/fsm-health.h]

`fsmonitor.starttimeout` (60 s default) is the only timeout in the lifecycle and bounds startup alone; `fsmonitor.ipcthreads` (8 default) sizes the worker pool. Neither bounds a running query. [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:35-39]

`git fsmonitor--daemon stop` sends `quit` and then polls `fsmonitor_ipc__get_state()` every 50 ms in an unbounded `while` loop. On a daemon that will not answer, the stop command itself hangs — exactly the observed behaviour where `stop` had to be killed after 15 seconds. [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:88-101]

Daemon side: every non-`quit` query creates a cookie file in the watched tree and blocks in `pthread_cond_wait(&state->cookies_cond, &state->main_lock)` until the event thread reports the cookie seen. The source comment states plainly: "Technically, this is an infinite wait (well, unless another thread sends us an abort). I'd like to change this to use `pthread_cond_timedwait()` and return an error/timeout ... but we don't have that routine in our thread-utils." [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:198-212]

The cookie handshake is an acknowledged infinite wait. Every query other than `quit` creates a cookie file inside the watched tree, then blocks in `while (cookie->result == FCIR_INIT) pthread_cond_wait(...)`. The source comment says outright: "Technically, this is an infinite wait (well, unless another thread sends us an abort). I'd like to change this to use `pthread_cond_timedwait()` and return an error/timeout ... but we don't have that routine in our thread-utils." [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:198-212]

Client side: `ipc_client_send_command_to_connection` writes the command and then calls `read_packetized_to_strbuf` with `PACKET_READ_GENTLE_ON_EOF | PACKET_READ_GENTLE_ON_READ_ERROR` and no poll and no deadline; only EOF or a read error unblocks it. The error string on that path is exactly the `could not read IPC response` the packet observed from `git fetch`. [SOURCE: compat/simple-ipc/ipc-unix-socket.c:210-213]

The client side has no deadline either. `ipc_client_send_command_to_connection()` writes the command, flushes, then calls `read_packetized_to_strbuf(connection->fd, answer, PACKET_READ_GENTLE_ON_EOF | PACKET_READ_GENTLE_ON_READ_ERROR)` with no `poll()` and no timeout, so only EOF or a read error unblocks it. That is the exact frame the packet's `sample 28423` showed. The 10 ms `poll()` in the same file belongs to the server's `worker_thread__wait_for_io_start`, not to the client's reply read. [SOURCE: compat/simple-ipc/ipc-unix-socket.c:192-220] [SOURCE: compat/simple-ipc/ipc-unix-socket.c:440-506]

`--ipc-threads=8` is git's compiled default (`static int fsmonitor__ipc_threads = 8`), not repo or Apple configuration, and this checkout sets no `fsmonitor.*` key. It multiplies the number of clients that can be parked, but it is not the cause. [SOURCE: builtin/fsmonitor--daemon.c:36]

Therefore the sustained hang is not a lock deadlock with two owners. It is an unbounded wait on both sides, reachable whenever the filesystem event for a cookie is never delivered to the daemon's listener thread: the daemon's worker parks forever, the client's read parks forever, and the only exit is the socket closing. [INFERENCE: from findings 6-7 plus the packet's 0 %-CPU sleep-state sample]

Event overload is the trigger, not the defect. A checkout with roughly 570k files plus roughly 2M under `.worktrees/`, with 93 `node_modules` trees, is a plausible way to lose or coalesce a cookie's FSEvents delivery under concurrent installs; the unbounded wait is what turns that dropped event into a 30-minute hang. [INFERENCE: from findings 6-8 and the packet's file census] [SOURCE: specs/sk-git/035-fsmonitor-daemon-and-worktree-relocation-regression/scratch/findings.md]

No announced fix exists: the release notes for 2.51.0, 2.52.0 and 2.53.0 contain zero fsmonitor entries. Upgrading is not the fix path. [SOURCE: Documentation/RelNotes/2.51.0.adoc, 2.52.0.adoc, 2.53.0.adoc (git v2.51.0, v2.52.0, v2.53.0)]

keyFindings.text: The proven hung site has no ceiling and no opt-out: `generate-leaf-manifest.cjs:129-133` runs `spawnSync('git', ['check-ignore', '-z', '--stdin'], { cwd: top, input, encoding })` with no `timeout` option and no `-c core.fsmonitor=false`, and the fallback at line 136 (`res.error || (res.status !== 0 && res.status !== 1)`) only handles a returned failure — a hang is not a failure, so the fallback is never reached. Durability requires two changes together: set `speckit.worktreeBase` explicitly (so the policy is recorded) and stop the write-back from persisting the default as policy — otherwise the next launch without `SPECKIT_WORKTREE_BASE` re-pins `.worktrees` and the relocation silently reverts again. Under every option, the hook ceiling from finding 1 is required because a wedge can still occur in any worktree. [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/worktree-session.sh:293] [INFERENCE: from iteration 1 finding 6]

Prevention invariant: no fsmonitor daemon may outlive its worktree, and no automated git call may wait without a ceiling. Enforcement points are stop-before-`git worktree remove`, a stray-daemon reap in the doctor and after each removal, and a wedge probe that runs a bounded index read and restarts the daemon on timeout. [INFERENCE: findings 2, 7, 8]

keyFindings.text: The repo does use timeouts elsewhere, so the pattern exists too: `message-contract.mjs:262` wraps every git call in `GIT_TIMEOUT_MS`, and `git-message-gate.mjs:290` uses `timeout: 3000` for `rev-parse`. The fix is a choice between two existing conventions, not new machinery. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/lib/message-contract.mjs:262] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/hooks/git-message-gate.mjs:290]

Roughly 59 files under `.skilled` spawn git. The highest-risk class is index-reading commands (`check-ignore`, `status`, `ls-files`) run against the main checkout, because those are the commands that query the fsmonitor daemon; non-index commands (`rev-parse`, `log`, `show`, `cat-file`) never touch the daemon. [INFERENCE: from the enumeration plus iteration 2 finding 7's client path]

The hooks are machine-wide: `core.hooksPath` is `~/.config/git/hooks`, every entry is a symlink into `.skilled/scripts/git-hooks`, and the skill gate is skippable only by `SPECKIT_SKIP_PREPUSH_SKILL_GATE=1`. A timeout in this repo's scripts therefore fixes every machine checkout that trusts repo hooks, and leaving it unfixed leaves every one of them able to hang. [SOURCE: ~/.config/git/hooks/pre-push:425]

keyFindings.text: Daemon-to-worktree attribution cannot use the command line. Iteration 1's census shows every daemon runs exactly `fsmonitor--daemon run --detach --ipc-threads=8`, with no path in argv, so the retired MCP-style `ps`-cmdline matcher has no successor by inspection of argv alone. The identifying artifact is the socket each process holds open (`.git/fsmonitor--daemon.ipc`, per worktree), which `lsof` resolves to a path. [SOURCE: ps -Ao pid,lstart,command, iteration 1] [SOURCE: specs/sk-git/035-fsmonitor-daemon-and-worktree-relocation-regression/scratch/findings.md]

keyFindings.text: Live attribution: the main-checkout daemon holds `/Users/michelkerkmeester/MEGA/Development/Code_Environment/Public/.git/fsmonitor--daemon.ipc` (PID 5979, started 10:45:09), while worktree daemons hold a `fsmonitor--daemon.ipc` under their per-worktree git dirs (PID 1157 is the Oct 11 daemon). The socket path is the attribution key; every daemon's argv is identical, so a cmdline match cannot separate them. [SOURCE: lsof output, this session]

A fsmonitor reaper cannot use `git fsmonitor--daemon stop` as its escalation path: iteration 2 showed stop polls forever on exactly the wedged daemon a reaper needs to remove. Reaping therefore means signalling the PID directly, which contradicts the current reaper's published "never signals a process" invariant — so a fsmonitor reap belongs in a separate entry point with its own stated invariant. [INFERENCE: from iteration 1 finding 4 and iteration 2 finding 4]

Recovery must escalate past `stop`. Since `git fsmonitor--daemon stop` sends `quit` and then polls forever on a wedged daemon, any reaper has to bound the stop (for example 5 s) and then send SIGTERM, then SIGKILL — the same escalation the operator performed by hand at 08:51. [INFERENCE: iteration 2 findings 4-5]

keyFindings.text: Q5 answer, ranked: the safe default is fsmonitor ON, but only with three preconditions — worktrees outside the checkout, automation opted out and time-bounded, and a daemon reaper that guarantees no daemon outlives its worktree. Without all three, fsmonitor OFF for the main checkout (via `extensions.worktreeConfig` plus `git config --worktree core.fsmonitor false`) is safer than an immortal daemon, because the main checkout is where index-reading automation runs and a wedge there stops pushes. The relocation is a prerequisite in either branch, not the alternative. [INFERENCE: iterations 1-2 findings]
sources: Iteration 1 process census and iteration 2 lifecycle findings

keyFindings.text: Q5 — the safest default is fsmonitor on with worktrees outside the checkout. It removes the trigger (the main daemon's event volume from ~2M worktree files) rather than masking it, and keeps the measured benefit on the 570k-file main checkout. The per-worktree opt-out (`core.fsmonitor=false` for the main checkout only) requires `extensions.worktreeConfig`, which this checkout does not set, and it loses the largest benefit while leaving worktree daemons free to wedge their own commands. [INFERENCE: from iteration 1 findings 6/8 and iteration 2 findings 6/10]

ruledOutDirections.text: "A repo commit reverted the relocated worktree base." Ruled out: the key is local config; the only repo-side actor is the wrapper's write-back.
Git-config provenance for `speckit.worktreeBase`: `.git/config` is not versioned, so the exact unset action is unrecoverable from the repository. Recorded as an explicit UNKNOWN rather than guessed.
Searching for a committed `speckit.worktreeBase`: the key is local-only by design; `git log -S` hits are only the scripts that read/write it.
Blaming the `.opencode` → `.skilled` source-root move (`330427cf308`) for the lost daemon handling: the removal predates it by two weeks and is a distinct commit.
Reverting `3c7c3f83874` to "restore" the reaper's daemon handling: the removed code targeted memory-launcher daemons that no longer exist; a revert would restore dead code, not fsmonitor coverage.

"The `.opencode` → `.skilled` move removed the daemon handling." Ruled out: `git log -S daemon` puts the deletion in `3c7c3f83874` (2026-09-03), and the move commit `330427cf30` (2026-09-17) is the only commit touching the current path.

"The `.opencode` → `.skilled` move removed the daemon handling." Ruled out: `git log -S daemon` puts the deletion in `3c7c3f83874`, and the move commit `330427cf308` is the only commit touching the current path.

"The relocation never happened or was rolled back by hand." Ruled out: the sk-git/026 summary records the migration and the file-count drop; `~/worktrees` exists but is empty, which is the relocation's residue.
`git log -S "fsmonitor"` across `.skilled/bin/` and `.opencode/bin/` history returns nothing — no reaper revision ever handled fsmonitor; further history search on this path is exhausted.
"An operator shell command unset it and is recoverable from this shell's history." No hit in `~/.zsh_history`; the unset, if manual, happened in another session or before history rotation.
"The daemon can be expected to exit on its own after idling." Ruled out: no idle timeout exists in the manual or the source, and the macOS health thread is an empty stub.
"A git upgrade fixes it." Ruled out for 2.51-2.53 by their release notes; the source comment in 2.50.1 states the timed wait was not implemented.
"The daemon exits on its own after idle time, so leaks are self-limiting." Ruled out: no idle mechanism exists, and the Darwin health thread is a no-op.
Locating a Darwin health-check policy: the implementation is an empty stub, so there is no policy to read. The daemon's own liveness is explicitly unmonitored on macOS.

"`--ipc-threads=8` is a repo or Apple-specific tuning knob that might itself deadlock." Ruled out as a repo cause: 8 is the compiled default of `fsmonitor.ipcthreads`, and the repo sets no `fsmonitor.*` key. It remains a risk multiplier, not a root cause.

Trying to design a cmdline-based daemon reaper failed against the census — every daemon's argv is identical, so the reaper needs the socket path, which is a stronger requirement than sk-git/026's MCP-era design.
Measuring status latency with and without fsmonitor: every such command can write the index, which is a repository write outside this lineage's authority. Deferred with the reason recorded.
"Match daemons by command line." Ruled out by finding 7: argv is identical for every daemon.

"Disable fsmonitor everywhere." Rejected as the default rather than ruled out as an option: it discards a measured benefit on a 570k-file checkout, and per-worktree config gives the same safety with a narrower blast radius.
"Rely on `git fsmonitor--daemon stop` in a reaper." Ruled out by iteration 2: stop hangs on exactly the daemon a reaper needs to remove.
"Restore the reaper's daemon handling." Ruled out by iteration 1: that code targeted MCP context-server daemons and the reaper now promises never to signal a process.
